paper_title: Color matters: Investigating stress recovery in VR-simulated interior environments using fNIRS and anxiety measures
abstract: Psychological stress is a growing global health concern, contributing to anxiety, burnout, and chronic illness. While traditional interventions focus on individual behaviors, environmental design-especially interior space where people spend most of their time-offers a scalable avenue for stress modulation. Among environmental stimuli, color is a powerful yet underutilized perceptual factor known to influence emotion and cognition. This study examines the impact of wall colors on acute stress recovery using a multimodal approach that combines immersive virtual reality (VR), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and self-reported anxiety assessments. A total of 38 participants were exposed to seven monochromatic colored-wall conditions (red, blue, orange, yellow, green, purple, and white), representing distinct hues across the visible color spectrum, during a 60-second post-stress recovery period. Brain activation in prefrontal regions and subjective anxiety levels were analyzed. Red and purple walls heightened activation in the DLPFC, PreM&SMC, and FEF, indicating increased cognitive control, motor readiness, and attentional vigilance, which aligned with elevated anxiety (p < .05). In contrast, white and blue reduced activation and supported emotional downregulation (p < .05), suggesting a restorative effect. Time-course analyses revealed early reactivity under red (0-20s) and delayed, stable responses under white (40-60s), highlighting color-specific modulation of stress-related neural functions and offering practical insights for designing stress-mitigating environments.–By integrating neural and behavioral evidence, the findings underscore the importance of color as a time-sensitive environmental variable, offering insights for the evidence-based design of stress-sensitive spaces.

methods_used: Immersive Virtual Reality (VR) using Oculus Quest 2 headset

Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) with a 67-channel instrument (KY-A, Wuhan YIRUIDE Group) to measure oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) and deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbR) concentrations, focusing on HbO.
Self-reported anxiety assessments using the short-form Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAIS-5)
Standardized cognitive stressor: Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task - Computerized (PASAT-C)
Color manipulation in HSL color space (Hue, Saturation, Lightness) with saturation and lightness held constant, and CIE Lab* values reported for perceptual consistency.
Data pre-processing with NIRS-KIT toolbox, linear detrending, Temporal Derivative Distribution Repair (TDDR) algorithm, Butterworth band-pass filter, and modified Beer-Lambert law.
Statistical analyses: Paired-samples t-tests, two-way Repeated Measures ANOVAs (Color × Time), Pearson correlation analyses, FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
regions_of_interest: Premotor and Supplementary Motor Cortex (PreM & SMC)

sample.demographics: 20 males, 18 females; age 21–33; right-handed university students with normal color vision, no neurological or psychiatric history, and prior experience with VR.

manipulated_features.feature_type: Wall color in VR-simulated interior environments
manipulated_features.control: Saturation and lightness were held constant across colors. Floor and ceiling remained a neutral gray tone.

neurophysiological: Changes in oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) concentrations in DLPFC, FPA, PreM&SMC, and FEF.
psychological: Subjective anxiety levels measured by STAIS-5 scores (before and after each color exposure).

key_findings.category: Stress Induction Validation (HbO activation during stress vs. baseline)
key_findings.details: All four ROIs exhibited significantly increased activation during the stress phase compared to baseline.

key_findings.category: Main Effect of Wall Color on Cortical Activation (HbO)
key_findings.details: A significant main effect of Color was found in DLPFC, PreM&SMC, and FEF.

effects.pairwise_comparison: Red > Orange/Yellow/Purple/White; Blue/Orange/Yellow/Green > White; Green > Purple

key_findings.category: Temporal Dynamics of Stress Recovery (HbO activation across time segments)
key_findings.details: A significant main effect of Time was observed in the PreM&SMC.

effects.pairwise_comparison: T2 (mid-recovery) > T1 (early recovery); T2 > T3 (late recovery)

key_findings.category: Interaction Effect (Color × Time) on Brain Activation (HbO)
key_findings.details: Significant Color × Time interaction effects were identified in DLPFC and FEF.

effects.pairwise_comparison: T1 (early recovery): Red > Blue/Green/White; T3 (late recovery): White > Purple

key_findings.details: Red and purple significantly increased anxiety compared to baseline. A significant main effect of Color was found.

key_findings.category: Correlations between HbO and STAIS-5 scores (exploratory findings)
key_findings.details: Several correlations reached statistical significance, but did not survive FDR correction for multiple comparisons.

mechanisms: Red and Purple hues: Heightened brain activation (DLPFC, PreM&SMC, FEF) indicating increased cognitive control, motor readiness, and attentional vigilance, aligning with elevated anxiety. Warm hues are associated with arousal and cognitive load, potentially sustaining or amplifying stress-related cognitive and emotional demands. Early FEF activation for red may reflect enhanced visual salience, alerting mechanisms, and threat detection.

White and Blue walls: Reduced cortical activation and supported emotional downregulation, suggesting a restorative effect and lower cortical activity and emotional stability. Low-arousal colors may facilitate restorative attention.

Yellow walls: Exhibited peak activation in the DLPFC during the mid-recovery phase (T2), suggesting a role in supporting cognitive stability in later recovery stages without significantly altering subjective anxiety.

Time-sensitive color impacts: Color-induced attentional and emotional effects follow a temporal arc, where high-salience hues exert early influence, and low-arousal hues modulate sustained regulation. Recovery is not a uniform process but features phase-specific cortical dynamics.
limitations: Fixed recovery duration (60 seconds) and limited exposure time per color may not capture long-term or cumulative effects.
Only fNIRS and self-report measures were used; incorporating physiological signals (e.g., heart rate, skin conductance) and real-world behavioral markers would provide a richer understanding.
Need for longer and adaptive exposure sequences.
Need to validate color timing strategies in real-world or clinical settings.
Individual differences in color-emotion associations were not fully explored.
design_implications: Color is a time-sensitive environmental variable for stress regulation, suggesting dynamic color design rather than static application.
Initiating recovery with calming hues (e.g., white or blue) and transitioning to stabilizing hues (e.g., yellow) can sustain cognitive and emotional regulation.
In healthcare settings (hospitals, clinics), exposure to blue or white environments during initial recovery may promote down-regulation of stress-related cortical activity.
In offices, dynamic lighting schemes that shift hue intensity across the day can be used to support attention and relaxation cycles.
Findings inform evidence-based design strategies for therapeutic, educational, and public spaces, as well as stress-relief rooms and adaptive VR environments.

environmental_features: VR-simulated interior environments with varying color schemes (e.g., different hues, saturation, or brightness levels)
Specific colors likely include restorative colors (e.g., blue, green) and potentially stimulating or neutral colors (e.g., red, grey)
control_conditions: VR-simulated interior environment with a neutral color scheme (e.g., grey or white)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Restorative environments, characterized by features like color, can facilitate recovery from directed attention fatigue and promote psychological well-being.
Exposure to certain environmental features, including color, can elicit physiological and psychological stress reduction responses.
Different colors evoke distinct psychological and physiological responses, influencing mood, emotion, and stress levels.

mechanism_chain.description: The color of VR-simulated interior environments influences stress recovery by modulating perceptual and affective responses, which are reflected in neural and physiological markers.
